tagline: Probably the earliest of Paul's surviving letters, written to a young and persecuted church to encourage it, instruct it in holiness, and comfort it about believers who had died.
overview:
First Thessalonians is very likely the oldest surviving letter of Paul, and so one of the oldest documents in the New Testament, written around AD 50, about twenty years after the death and resurrection of Jesus. Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to a church he had founded only months before in Thessalonica, the leading city of Macedonia. He had been forced to leave suddenly, the new believers faced hostility from their neighbors, and he had no way of knowing whether their faith had survived. When Timothy returned with good news, Paul wrote this letter of relief, thanks, and encouragement.

The first three chapters are personal. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians turned to God from idols, recalls how he and his companions lived among them like a nursing mother and a father, defends the sincerity of their conduct, and explains how desperately he wanted to see them again. The last two chapters give instruction: live in holiness and sexual purity, love one another, work quietly with your own hands, and do not grieve over believers who have died as if you had no hope, because the Lord will come and the dead in Christ will rise. The Day of the Lord will come like a thief, so stay awake and sober, and live together as a church in peace, joy, prayer, and thanks.

The letter shows the Christian faith in its earliest written form, and it already contains the heart of it: God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit; Jesus' death and resurrection; turning from idols to the living God; and waiting for his Son from heaven. Its triad of faith, love, and hope (1:3; 5:8) sets the tone for everything after.
author: Paul wrote 1 Thessalonians, with Silvanus (the Silas of Acts) and Timothy named alongside him (1:1). Its authenticity is accepted by nearly all scholars. The letter's warmth, its detailed memories of the founding visit, and its fit with the account in Acts 17 all point to Paul, and it was included in the earliest collections of his letters. Although three names stand in the greeting and the letter often says we, Paul speaks in the first person at key moments (2:18; 3:5; 5:27), which shows him as its principal author.
date: Paul wrote from Corinth, shortly after Timothy rejoined him there (3:6; compare Acts 18:5). Paul's stay in Corinth can be dated fairly closely because Acts 18:12 places the proconsul Gallio there during it, and an inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term in Achaia to about AD 51 to 52. That places the letter around AD 50 or 51, making it very likely Paul's earliest surviving letter. The one serious rival is Galatians, which some scholars date around AD 48 on the view that it was written to churches in southern Galatia before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15; most who date Galatians later regard 1 Thessalonians as the earliest.
setting:
Thessalonica was founded around 316 BC by Cassander, one of the successors of Alexander the Great, who named it after his wife Thessalonike, Alexander's half-sister. It had a fine harbor on the Thermaic Gulf and stood on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road that crossed the Balkans, so trade, travelers, and news passed through it constantly. When Rome organized Macedonia as a province in the 140s BC, Thessalonica became its capital. Because it sided with Antony and Octavian in the civil war of 42 BC, it was rewarded as a free city, governed by its own magistrates, whom Acts calls politarchs (Acts 17:6), a title confirmed by inscriptions from the city. The city honored Rome and its emperors, and it was home to many cults, including Egyptian gods, Dionysus, and the local cult of Cabirus, as well as a Jewish synagogue.

Acts 17:1-10 tells the story of the church's founding on Paul's second missionary trip, around AD 49 or 50, after he and Silas had been beaten and jailed in Philippi (compare 1 Thessalonians 2:2). For three Sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and some Jews, a large number of God-fearing Greeks, and a number of leading women believed. Opposition then stirred up a mob, which dragged Jason, Paul's host, before the city officials and accused the missionaries of defying Caesar's decrees by saying there is another king, Jesus. Paul and Silas were sent away by night to Berea and then Paul went on to Athens and Corinth. The letter itself suggests the church was largely Gentile, since its members had turned to God from idols (1:9), and that Paul had stayed long enough to work at his trade and to receive gifts from Philippi more than once (2:9; Philippians 4:16).
purpose: Paul writes, first, out of relief and love: to thank God for the church's faith under pressure and to renew the bond that had been broken by his sudden departure (2:17 to 3:10). Second, he defends his own conduct, apparently against suggestions that he had been one more traveling speaker out for money or praise who abandoned his followers (2:1-12). Third, he gives instruction the young church needed: on sexual holiness in a culture with very different standards, on brotherly love and daily work, on the fate of believers who had died before the Lord's coming, on readiness for the Day of the Lord, and on the life of the congregation (chapters 4 and 5).
story: First Thessalonians fills out the brief account of Acts 17 and shows what happened after Paul left a city. It stands at the point where the gospel had just crossed from Asia into Europe, through Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, and Corinth. In the larger story of the Bible it shows Gentiles turning from idols to the living God, as the prophets had said the nations would, and it looks forward to the coming of the Lord, the Day of the Lord announced by the prophets from Amos onward, now understood as the return of Jesus. Second Thessalonians follows closely and continues the same conversation.
christ: Even in this early letter, Jesus is spoken of in the same breath as God the Father, the church's life being in both together (1:1) and as the one who, with the Father, can direct Paul's way (3:11). He is God's Son, raised from the dead, who rescues believers from the coming wrath (1:10). He died for us so that we may live together with him (5:10). His coming, the parousia, is the horizon of the whole letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23). Believers who have died are the dead in Christ, and the end of the story is that we will always be with the Lord (4:16-17).
reading: Read 1 Thessalonians as a pastor's letter to new converts, full of emotion and memory as well as instruction. Watch for the repeated you know, as Paul reminds the church of what they already experienced and were taught, and for the triad of faith, love, and hope. Notice how often teaching about the Lord's coming is tied to comfort and to conduct rather than to calculation. The passage on the dead in Christ (4:13-18) is central to later debates about the rapture and the order of end-time events; read it first for what Paul says it is for, that believers may encourage one another and not grieve as those without hope, before asking how it fits a larger scheme.

structure.title: Thanksgiving for the church
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians' faith, love, and hope, and for how they welcomed the gospel and turned from idols to serve the living God.

structure.title: Paul's conduct among them
structure.summary: Paul recalls how he and his companions preached with integrity, lived gently among them, and worked night and day, and thanks God that they received the word of God.

structure.title: Paul's longing and Timothy's report
structure.summary: Kept away by force, Paul sent Timothy to strengthen them; Timothy's good news brings him joy, and he prays to see them and for their love to grow.

structure.title: Living to please God
structure.summary: Instruction on sexual holiness, brotherly love, and a quiet life of work that earns the respect of outsiders.

structure.title: The Lord's coming
structure.summary: The dead in Christ will rise and all believers will be with the Lord; the Day of the Lord will come like a thief, so live as children of the day.

structure.title: Life together and farewell
structure.summary: Respect leaders, care for one another, rejoice, pray, give thanks, test prophecy, and receive a closing blessing.

themes.title: Faith, love, and hope
themes.body: Paul thanks God for the church's work of faith, labor of love, and enduring hope (1:3), and later describes faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet (5:8). The three words, which appear together again in 1 Corinthians 13:13, summarize the Christian life as trust in God, love for others, and confident waiting for Christ.

themes.title: The coming of the Lord
themes.body: Every chapter closes on or near a reference to the Lord's return. Paul uses the word parousia, the term for a ruler's arrival or official visit, and he speaks of it as the believers' hope, the time when their faithfulness will be revealed, and the reunion of the living with those who have died. It is also the Day of the Lord, which will come suddenly on those who are not ready.

themes.title: Suffering and endurance
themes.body: The church received the word in much affliction (1:6), and Paul reminds them that he warned them trials would come (3:3-4). Their perseverance under pressure is evidence of God's work. The letter does not explain suffering away; it sets it within the pattern of Jesus, the prophets, and the churches in Judea, and within the hope of his coming.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.body: God's will is the church's sanctification (4:3). Holiness in this letter is practical: sexual purity, honesty in dealings, love, and hard work, and it is also God's own work, since Paul prays that the God of peace will sanctify them completely (5:23). The Spirit given to them is called holy (4:8).

themes.title: A pastor's love
themes.body: No letter of Paul shows more openly the affection between a missionary and a young church. He compares himself to a nursing mother and a father, speaks of being orphaned when separated from them, and says he can go on living now that he knows they stand firm. The letter models ministry as shared life, not only shared message (2:8).

keyChapters.why: A compact picture of conversion in the first generation: the gospel coming in power and the Spirit, and Gentiles turning from idols to serve God and await his Son.
Paul's account of how he and his companions conducted themselves, one of the fullest pictures of his ministry and motives in any of his letters.
Instruction on holiness and daily work, and the passage on believers who have died and the Lord's coming (4:13-18).
The Day of the Lord coming like a thief, and a series of brief commands for church life, including rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks.

parts.body:
1 Thessalonians is a letter from Paul, with his friends Silvanus and Timothy, to a young church in Thessalonica, a busy port city in northern Greece. It has 5 chapters and can be read aloud in about fifteen minutes.

It is very likely the oldest letter of Paul that we have, and so one of the oldest pieces of writing in the whole New Testament. It was written around AD 50, about twenty years after Jesus died and rose.

Paul had founded the church only a few months before. Then trouble broke out, and he had to leave the city by night. He left behind a handful of new believers, most of them people who had worshipped idols until a few weeks earlier, and their neighbours were now making life hard for them. Paul did not know whether their faith would last. He sent Timothy back to find out. When Timothy came back with good news, Paul wrote this letter, full of relief and love.

The first half (chapters 1 to 3) looks back. Paul thanks God for the way they turned from idols ‘to serve the living and true God’ (1:9), and he reminds them how he lived among them, gentle as a nursing mother and caring as a father. The second half (chapters 4 and 5) looks ahead. Live a holy life. Love one another and work with your hands. And do not lose hope over believers who have died, because the Lord Jesus will come, and the dead in Christ will rise.

The letter is short and warm, and it holds some of the plainest words in the Bible about death and hope. “And so we will always be with the Lord” (4:17). Paul's reason for writing them down is just as plain: “Therefore encourage one another with these words” (4:18).

The letter opens with three names: “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy” (1:1). Silvanus is the longer, Latin form of the name Silas, the man from the church in Jerusalem who travelled with Paul on this trip (Acts 15:22, 40). Timothy had joined them a little earlier, at Lystra (Acts 16:1-3).

The letter often says ‘we’, and the three were together when the church began. But at a few key moments Paul speaks for himself: “indeed I, Paul, tried again and again” (2:18). So Paul is the main writer, with his two friends standing beside him.

Almost no one doubts that Paul wrote it. Scholars of every kind accept it as his. The letter's warm memories of the first visit, its style, and the way it fits the story in Acts 17 all point to him, and it was part of the earliest collections of his letters.

parts.h: Thessalonica, and how the church began
parts.body:
Thessalonica was founded around 316 BC by Cassander, one of the generals who took over after Alexander the Great died. He named the city after his wife, Thessalonike, who was Alexander's half-sister. It had a fine harbour, and it stood on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road that ran across the Balkans. Trade, travellers and news passed through it all the time. When Rome made Macedonia a province in the 140s BC, Thessalonica became its capital. In the Roman civil war of 42 BC it took the winning side, and it was rewarded by being made a free city, run by its own officials. Acts calls them ‘city officials’ (Acts 17:6), and their Greek title has been found on inscriptions in the city itself.

The city honoured Rome and its emperors. It had temples to many gods, among them Egyptian gods, Dionysus, and a local god called Cabirus. It also had a Jewish synagogue.

Acts tells how the church began, around AD 49 or 50 (Acts 17:1-10). Paul and Silas came on from Philippi, where they had been beaten and thrown into prison. For three Sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures, “explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead” (Acts 17:3). Some Jews believed, along with “a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women” (Acts 17:4). Others in the synagogue opposed them, and with some troublemakers from the marketplace they stirred up the city. A mob dragged Paul's host, Jason, before the officials, with the charge that the missionaries said “there is another king, named Jesus” (Acts 17:7). That night the believers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea.

The letter adds things Acts does not tell. Most of the church had worshipped idols (1:9), so it was mostly Gentile. Paul stayed long enough to work at his trade ‘night and day’ (2:9), and long enough for the church in Philippi to send him help more than once (Philippians 4:16). And after he left, the new believers suffered ‘from your own countrymen’ (2:14), their Gentile neighbours.

parts.h: When and where it was written
parts.body:
From Berea Paul was taken to Athens. He was so anxious about the Thessalonians that he sent Timothy back to them, though it meant being left alone (3:1-2). Timothy later returned with good news (3:6). Acts says that Silas and Timothy came to Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and that is where most think Paul wrote this letter.

The time can be fixed quite closely. While Paul was in Corinth, he was brought before the governor Gallio (Acts 18:12). An inscription found at Delphi, in Greece, dates Gallio's time in office to about AD 51 to 52. That places this letter around AD 50 or 51.

That makes it very likely the earliest of Paul's letters to survive. The one serious rival is Galatians, which some date a little earlier. Either way, when you read 1 Thessalonians you are reading the Christian faith in one of its very first written forms. And it is all already here: God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit, Jesus' death and resurrection, and the hope of his coming.

Thanks for a young church (chapter 1). Paul thanks God for their ‘work of faith’, ‘labor of love’ and ‘enduring hope’ (1:3), and for the way the news of their turning to God has spread.

How Paul lived among them (2:1-16). Not like the travelling speakers who were after money and praise. He was gentle like a nursing mother, worked night and day so as not to be a burden, and cared for each of them like a father. They received his message as the word of God, and they suffered for it, as the churches in Judea had.

Longing and good news (2:17 to 3:13). Torn away from them, Paul longed to come back. He sent Timothy instead, and Timothy has returned with good news. Paul's joy spills over into a prayer.

A life that pleases God (4:1-12). Be holy, especially in sexual life. Love one another. Live quietly and work with your own hands.

The Lord's coming (4:13 to 5:11). Do not grieve over believers who have died as if there were no hope. The Lord will come, the dead in Christ will rise, and all his people will be with him. The Day of the Lord will come like a thief, so stay awake and live as children of the day.

Life together, and goodbye (5:12-28). Respect your leaders, care for the weak, rejoice, pray, give thanks, test everything. Then a prayer, a blessing and a farewell.

Notice that every chapter ends near the same place: the coming of the Lord Jesus (1:10; 2:19; 3:13; 4:17; 5:23).

parts.h: The Lord's coming: what all confess, and where Christians differ
parts.body:
Some of the believers in Thessalonica had died since Paul left. The living were grieving, and they seem to have feared that those who died had missed out on the Lord's coming. Paul writes to comfort them. He does not tell them not to grieve. He tells them not to grieve “like the rest, who are without hope” (4:13).

The ground of his comfort is Easter: “For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him” (4:14). Then he describes the Lord's coming. The Lord will come down from heaven with a loud command and the trumpet of God. The dead in Christ will rise first. Then the living “will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord” (4:16-17).

The church has always confessed what these verses teach: that Jesus Christ will come again, that the dead will be raised, and that he will judge the living and the dead. Every Christian tradition holds this. It is not one view among several.

Where Christians differ is the order of events. The word ‘caught up’ became ‘rapture’ in English by way of the Latin Bible. Some Christians read these verses as a coming of Christ for his church, who are caught up to be with him before a time of great trouble, often thought of as seven years; after it, he returns openly with them. They point out that the passage says nothing of trouble coming first, and that ‘God has not appointed us to suffer wrath’ (5:9). Others believe the church will be caught up in the middle of that time, or before the worst of God's wrath falls. Others read these verses as the church being caught up at Christ's one, open return after the time of trouble. The word for ‘meet’ was often used when a city's people went out to welcome an arriving ruler and walk back in with him, and they think Paul pictures believers going out to welcome their King as he comes. And many Christians, in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and other churches, do not separate a rapture from the return at all. For them this is the one coming of Christ at the end of the age, with the resurrection and the judgment, and they note that a loud command and a trumpet are hardly secret.

These notes do not choose. Faithful Christians hold each of these views. The site's study on the end times sets them out more fully, each as its holders would put it.

And Paul gives no date. He says the Day will come “like a thief in the night” (5:2), and he tells the church how to live, not when to expect it. No one should set a date for the Lord's return, or say that a particular event of our own time is the one these verses describe. Paul wrote these words to comfort grieving people, and that is what they are for.

In chapter 2 Paul tells the Thessalonians that they have suffered from their own countrymen, just as the churches in Judea suffered ‘from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and drove us out as well’ (2:14-15). These are some of the hardest words in Paul's letters, and they must be read with great care.

First, notice who is speaking. Paul is a Jew. Jesus was a Jew. The first apostles were Jews. The churches in Judea that Paul speaks of were made up of Jews. Paul himself had once been one of those who hunted the church in Judea (Galatians 1:13, 22-23).

Second, notice what he is comparing. The Thessalonians, who were Gentiles, suffered from their Gentile neighbours. The Judean believers, who were Jews, suffered from some of their Jewish neighbours. Paul is speaking of particular people in particular places who fought against the gospel and drove out its messengers. He is comparing persecutors with persecutors, not one people with another.

Third, set these words beside what Paul says elsewhere. Of his own people he writes, “For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood” (Romans 9:3). And he asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1).

These verses are not a verdict on the Jewish people, then or now. For centuries some Christians used words like these to teach contempt for Jews, to blame them for the death of Jesus, and to justify cruelty against them. That reading is false, and this site rejects it plainly. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why.

Faith, love and hope. Paul thanks God for their ‘work of faith’, ‘labor of love’ and ‘enduring hope’ (1:3). In chapter 5 the same three become armour: “putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation” (5:8). Trust in God, love for others, and waiting for Christ: that is the whole Christian life in three words.

Turning to God. The Thessalonians turned ‘to God from idols’ (1:9). In their world that was costly. Family meals, trade guilds and city festivals all honoured the gods, and a person who stopped could look disloyal and even dangerous. Turning to God meant turning their whole life around.

Suffering. They ‘welcomed the message with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering’ (1:6). Paul had warned them it would come (3:4). The letter does not explain suffering away. It puts them in a long line with Jesus, the prophets and the churches of Judea.

Holiness. “For it is God’s will that you should be holy” (4:3). Holiness here is practical: sexual faithfulness, honesty, love and steady work. And it is God's own work, for Paul prays that “the God of peace Himself” will make them holy through and through (5:23).

The coming of the Lord. Paul uses a word, parousia, that was used for the arrival of a ruler on an official visit. The Lord's coming is the church's hope, the day their lives will be seen for what they are, and the day the living and the dead in Christ will be together with him.

A pastor's love. No letter shows more openly the love between Paul and a church. He was ‘like a nursing mother’ (2:7) and like a father (2:11). When he was taken from them, he uses a Greek word for being orphaned (2:17). And when good news came, he wrote, “For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord” (3:8).

This letter does not quote the Old Testament word for word. Its readers were mostly new believers from a world of idols. But it is full of the language of Israel's Scriptures.

‘The living and true God’ (1:9) is how the prophets spoke of the LORD against the idols. “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King” (Jeremiah 10:10). The idols, a psalm says, “have mouths, but cannot speak” (Psalm 115:5).

‘Be holy’ goes back to the law: “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). When Paul says the Thessalonians have been ‘taught by God’ to love (4:9), he may be echoing the promise that “all your sons will be taught by the LORD” (Isaiah 54:13). And when he says God ‘gives you His Holy Spirit’ (4:8), he echoes Ezekiel: “And I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27).

The Lord's coming is told in pictures from the Old Testament. The trumpet and the clouds recall Sinai, where “A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out” (Exodus 19:16), and Daniel's vision of “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13). The rising of the dead is the hope of Isaiah: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19).

‘The Day of the Lord’ (5:2) is the prophets' name for the day God acts to judge and to save. Amos warned those who longed for it that it would be “darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18). The cry of ‘Peace and security’ (5:3) sounds like the false prophets who said ‘Peace, peace,’ “when there is no peace at all” (Jeremiah 6:14). And the armour of 5:8 comes from Isaiah, where God himself “put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head” (Isaiah 59:17).

The most striking echo is in 3:13. Zechariah said, “Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him” (Zechariah 14:5). Paul speaks of ‘the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints’. What the prophet said of the LORD, Paul says of Jesus.

It is not a timetable. Paul answers questions about ‘times and seasons’ (5:1) by telling the church how to live, not by giving a date. Jesus himself said, “No one knows about that day or hour” (Matthew 24:36). Anyone who sets a date for the Lord's coming, or names a living person, a nation or an event of our own day as the fulfilment of these chapters, goes beyond what the letter says. Many such predictions have come and gone, and they have hurt the faith of people who trusted them.

It is not a reason to stop grieving. Paul tells grieving people that they do not grieve without hope. He does not tell them their grief is wrong. Jesus himself wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35).

It is not contempt for the Jewish people. The part above on 2:14-16 says why.

It is not contempt for anyone in the matter of sex. Paul calls the church to sexual holiness (4:3-8), and he speaks plainly. But his words are a call to people inside the church, not a weapon against people outside it, and they give no one leave for contempt toward any person.

And it is not a reason to withdraw from the world. Paul tells believers to live quietly and work with their own hands so that they ‘behave properly toward outsiders’ (4:12), and to ‘pursue what is good for one another and for all people’ (5:15). Waiting for the Lord means living well among your neighbours, not leaving them behind.

Read it in one sitting, as a letter from a pastor to new believers he loves and worries about. It reads best that way.

Watch for the words that come back: ‘you know’ and ‘you remember’, as Paul reminds them of what they saw with their own eyes; faith, love and hope; holiness; and the coming of the Lord.

Notice how much feeling there is. Paul is relieved, grateful, anxious, and full of longing. He is not writing a book of doctrine. He is writing to friends.

Notice what the teaching about the end is for. Every time Paul speaks of the Lord's coming, he ties it to comfort or to how to live: stay awake, be sober, encourage one another. Read 4:13-18 first for what Paul says it is for, before asking how it fits a larger plan.

And let the letter ask you its questions. What have you turned from, and what have you turned to? Who has loved you the way Paul loved this church? Whom are you grieving, and where is your hope? And if the Lord came today, would he find you awake?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘Gentle among you’, or ‘infants among you’? One letter in Greek, and why both readings say the same thing about Paul.
Paul's hard words about those who opposed the gospel in Judea. Why they are no verdict on the Jewish people, then or now.
‘Satan obstructed us.’ What Paul meant, and what he did next.
‘God’s will that you should be holy.’ Sexual holiness, stated plainly and without contempt for any person.
‘Caught up … to meet the Lord in the air.’ What all Christians confess, and the main readings of the rapture and the return.
‘We who are alive and remain.’ Did Paul expect to be alive when the Lord came?
‘Like a thief in the night.’ Why the Day of the Lord comes with no date attached.
‘Spirit, soul, and body.’ Three parts of a person, or the whole person?

words.line: The word for a ruler's arrival on an official visit. Paul uses it for the return of Jesus (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23).
The prophets' name for the day God acts to judge and to save. Paul ties it to the coming of Jesus (5:2).
Greek epistrephō, to turn around. The Thessalonians ‘turned to God from idols’ (1:9). Conversion is a change of direction.
How the prophets named the LORD over against idols, which cannot speak or act (1:9; Jeremiah 10:10).
God's settled opposition to evil, which will come on the Day of the Lord. Jesus is ‘our deliverer from the coming wrath’ (1:10).
A gentle way of speaking of death, in Jewish and Greek speech alike. For Christians it means those who sleep will wake (4:13-15).
Greek harpazō, to snatch up suddenly. The Latin Bible's word here gives English the word ‘rapture’ (4:17). The word itself says nothing about timing.
Greek apantēsis. Often used when a city's people went out to welcome an arriving ruler and escort him back in (4:17).
Being set apart for God, in body and in conduct. ‘For it is God’s will that you should be holy’ (4:3).
To make holy. Paul prays that the God of peace will sanctify them ‘completely’, the whole person (5:23).
The Latin form of the name Silas, Paul's companion on this trip (Acts 15:40). He is named first after Paul (1:1).

timeline.what: Cassander founds Thessalonica and names it after his wife, Alexander the Great's half-sister.
Rome makes Macedonia a province, and Thessalonica becomes its capital.
Thessalonica takes the winning side in Rome's civil war and is made a free city with its own officials.
After being beaten and jailed in Philippi, Paul and Silas come to Thessalonica. The church begins, then they are sent away by night (Acts 17:1-10).
Paul goes on to Berea and Athens, and sends Timothy back from Athens to strengthen the church (3:1-2).
Timothy rejoins Paul in Corinth with good news (3:6; Acts 18:5). Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, very likely his earliest surviving letter.
Gallio governs the province of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul is brought before him in Corinth (Acts 18:12).
Paul writes again to the same church. Many hold that 2 Thessalonians followed within weeks or months; some think it was written later.

places.line: Capital of Macedonia, a port on the great Roman road. The church Paul founded here had to watch him leave by night (1:1; Acts 17:1-10).

places.name: Athens
places.line: Where Paul was willing to be left alone, so that he could send Timothy back to the Thessalonians (3:1-2).

places.name: Corinth
places.line: Where Timothy brought Paul good news, and where Paul most likely wrote this letter (3:6; Acts 18:5).

teaching.mapNote: Paul came to Thessalonica from Philippi, along the great Roman road. Driven out, he went on by way of Berea to Athens, and then to Corinth, where he wrote this letter.
